---
title: "Shadow"
slug: shadow
order: 17
permalink: /books/meat-bibles-symbolic-language/shadow/
description: "A prime example of a symbol read backwards — and the backwards reading props up a doctrine: the most-quoted verse for the claim that the commandments are done away calls them 'a shadow of things to come.' But shadow-as-gloom is the reader's assumption, not Scripture's usage: in Scripture the shadow is the covering of a greater presence — the shadow of the Almighty, of His wings, of a kingdom's tree over its peoples — and the KJV itself twice renders the word 'defence.' The law is a shadow of GOOD things; a shadow is attached to the body that casts it and falls where the body is found; and the verse's own command is 'let no man judge you' for keeping the feasts — which ARE, present tense, a shadow of things still to come. It is good to be in the shadow; the question is whose."
og_title: "Shadow — MEAT The Bible's Symbolic Language"
epigraphs:
  - quote: "He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty."
    ref: "Psalm 91:1"
---
Say the word __“shadow”__ and gloom answers — and on that gloom an entire doctrine has been built.
Ask why the commandments no longer bind, and the verse quoted most in answer is a shadow verse:

[quote.scripture, Colossians 2:16-17]
____
Let no man therefore sym:sym-judgment[judge] *you* in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an *holyday*, or of the *new* sym:sym-moon[moon], or of the *sabbath days*: Which are a *shadow of things to come*; but the *body* is of Christ.
____

The teaching runs: the sabbaths and feasts were only shadows pointing ahead to Christ; the substance has come, so the shadows are discharged — who keeps company with a shadow once the body has arrived?
Every step of that reading leans on a single assumption: that a shadow is a poor and dispensable thing — gloom, a lesser copy, a something-less-than.
The assumption is the reader's, not Scripture's.

This chapter gathers every use of the word — it falls in some eighty verses — and finds the shadow is not the danger and not the discount: the shadow is the *shelter*.
Hold the verdict on Colossians until the evidence is in; the verse will be waiting further down this road, and by then it will read as the opposite of a discharge.

Begin where the King James itself lets the meaning slip through in plain English.
When Joshua and Caleb plead with Israel not to fear the Canaanites, listen to the word they choose:

[quote.scripture, Numbers 14:9]
____
Only rebel not ye against the LORD, neither fear ye the people of the land; for they are sym:sym-bread[bread] for us: their *defence* is departed from them, and the LORD is with us: fear them not.
____

__“Their defence”__ is the Hebrew _tsel_ — their *shadow*.
The nations’ shadow has departed, and a people stripped of its shadow stands naked to judgment.
Solomon uses the same word the same way: __“sym:sym-wisdom[wisdom] is a defence, and money is a defence”__ (Ecclesiastes 7:12) — in the Hebrew, a man shelters _in the shadow_ of wisdom as in the shadow of money.

Twice the translators reached for __“defence”__ because the sense demanded it: in Scripture, a shadow is a covering that protects.
That is the habit to carry from this page: when the English wobbles between renderings, the wobble is a signpost — look beneath it.

The righteous live under a different shadow.

[quote.scripture, Psalm 91:1]
____
He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the *shadow of the Almighty*.
____

[quote.scripture, Psalm 36:7]
____
How excellent is thy lovingkindness, O God! therefore the children of men put their trust under the *shadow of thy* sym:sym-wings[wings].
____

The shadow of His sym:sym-wings[wings] is where David hides (Psalm 17:8), makes his refuge until calamities pass (Psalm 57:1), and rejoices (Psalm 63:7) — and those wings are the _kanaph_, the edge link:/books/symbolic-language/wings/[where the fringe is bound] as the reminder of the commandments (Numbers 15:38-39).footnote:fn13kanaph[Derived in the link:/books/symbolic-language/wings/[Wings] chapter.]
__“The LORD is thy keeper: the LORD is thy *shade* upon thy right hand”__ (Psalm 121:5) — the LORD does not merely cast a shadow; He _is_ the shade.
And Isaiah sets the definition in parallel columns — Scripture’s habit of defining a term by saying the thing twice:

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 25:4]
____
For thou hast been a strength to the sym:sym-poor[poor], a strength to the needy in his distress, a *refuge from the* sym:sym-storm[storm], a *shadow from the heat*, when the blast of the terrible ones is as a sym:sym-storm[storm] against the wall.
____

Refuge answers shadow; storm answers heat.
So too the shadow of a great sym:sym-rock[rock] (Isaiah 32:2); the tabernacle is __“for a shadow in the daytime from the heat, and for a place of refuge”__ (Isaiah 4:6).
The Servant testifies, __“in the shadow of his hand hath he hid me”__ (Isaiah 49:2), and God answers Zion, __“I have covered thee in the shadow of mine hand… Thou art my people”__ (Isaiah 51:16).
The bride sits under her beloved’s shadow with delight (Song of Solomon 2:3).
The prodigal nation comes home to it: __“They that dwell under his shadow shall return; they shall revive”__ (Hosea 14:7).
And under the anointed king’s shadow Israel shall live among the heathen (Lamentations 4:20).

Trust, hiding, delight, revival, life among the nations — that is the shadow’s company in Scripture.
It is good to be in the shadow.

Shade from what?
Read the refuge verses again and notice what the shadow shields from: the heat.
__“The LORD is thy shade… the sym:sym-sun[sun] shall not smite thee by day”__ (Psalm 121:5-6).

At full strength, the heat in Scripture is not the weather: __“our God is a consuming fire”__ (Deuteronomy 4:24; Hebrews 12:29).
Isaiah asks the question outright — __“Who among us shall dwell with the devouring fire? who among us shall dwell with everlasting burnings?”__ — and answers it: __“He that walketh righteously”__ (Isaiah 33:14-15).
To live near God is to live near the fire, and only the covered live there.

Moses himself was shaded so: __“I will put thee in a clift of the sym:sym-rock[rock], and will cover thee with my hand while I pass by”__ (Exodus 33:22) — the shadow of God’s own hand set between a man and God’s own glory.
And whose hand is that?
The hand of the LORD is the hand that saves: __“his right hand, and his holy arm, hath gotten him the victory”__ (Psalm 98:1) — where __“gotten the victory”__ is the Hebrew _yasha_: His right hand works _yeshuah_.
The hand-shadow set between a man and the glory is God’s own salvation — Yeshua — standing in the gap; it was the Servant who said, __“in the shadow of his hand hath he hid me”__ (Isaiah 49:2).

One psalm says both halves in a single breath: __“the LORD God is a sym:sym-sun[sun] and shield”__ (Psalm 84:11) — the Sun and the shield from it, the fire and the covering, in one Person.
He shades us from Himself, and the shade is His Messiah.

Now the equation closes, because we already know where the covering hangs.
The shadow the psalms trust is the shadow of the wings, and Psalm 91 lays the two lines side by side: __“under the shadow of the Almighty… under his sym:sym-wings[wings] shalt thou trust”__ (Psalm 91:1, 4).
The sym:sym-wings[wings] are the _kanaph_, the covenant corners where the sym:sym-tzitzit[tassels] are bound to remind the wearer of the commandments — and it is the cherubim’s wings that shadow the mercy seat (Hebrews 9:5).
Wings, shade, commands: one covering.

The commandments are not the fire; they are the shade that lets a man dwell beside it — which is why the same Sun that smites the uncovered rises __“with healing in his sym:sym-wings[wings]”__ on them that fear His sym:sym-name[name] (Malachi 4:2).
It is good to be in the shadow, because the alternative is not the open sky; it is the open blaze.

The symbol scales up, exactly as the sea and the mountain did.
A kingdom is a sym:sym-tree[tree], and a tree casts shade: a kingdom’s shadow is its protection spread over peoples.
When Jotham told the trees’ parable of kingship, the offer of the crown was an offer of shade:

[quote.scripture, Judges 9:15]
____
And the sym:sym-bramble[bramble] said unto the sym:sym-tree[trees], If in truth ye anoint me king over you, then come and *put your trust in my shadow*: and if not, let *fire* come out of the bramble, and devour the sym:sym-cedar[cedars] of Lebanon.
____

Ezekiel draws the empire of Assyria as a cedar, and names what its shadow held:

[quote.scripture, Ezekiel 31:6]
____
All the fowls of heaven made their nests in his boughs, and under his sym:sym-branches[branches] did all the sym:sym-beast[beasts] of the field bring forth their young, and *under his shadow dwelt all great nations*.
____

When the cedar falls, __“all the people of the earth are gone down from his shadow”__ (Ezekiel 31:12).
Nebuchadnezzar’s tree gave the beasts of the field shadow (Daniel 4:12); God’s own planted cedar shelters __“all fowl of every wing… in the shadow of the branches”__ (Ezekiel 17:23); and the kingdom of heaven grows into the mustard tree __“so that the fowls of the air may lodge under the shadow of it”__ (Mark 4:32).
Every kingdom is a shadow-offer; that is what a kingdom _is_ to the people under it.

Which is why the false shadow is a snare.
Judah ran from Assyria to __“trust in the shadow of sym:sym-egypt[Egypt]”__ — and God answered, __“the trust in the shadow of Egypt”__ shall be __“your confusion”__ (Isaiah 30:2-3).
Israel spread her idolatry __“under oaks and poplars and elms, *because the shadow thereof is good*”__ (Hosea 4:13) — even sin is shadow-hunger; the idolater is a man sheltering under the wrong tree.

Everyone lives in some shadow.
The question Scripture presses is whose.

There is a Presence in this shadow, and the thread runs from the tabernacle to the gospels.
When the cloud of glory settled on the finished tabernacle, the Greek Old Testament says it _overshadowed_ it — _epeskiazen_ (Exodus 40:35) — and that is the very verb the New Testament keeps reaching for.
At the transfiguration, __“a bright cloud overshadowed them”__ (Matthew 17:5) — brightness that shades.
The sick were laid in the street __“that at the least the shadow of Peter passing by might overshadow some of them”__ (Acts 5:15).
And at the head of the gospel:

[quote.scripture, Luke 1:35]
____
And the angel answered and said unto her, The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall *overshadow* thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God.
____

The Son was conceived under the overshadowing — the same covering cloud that filled the tabernacle came down over a virgin in Nazareth.
The shadow of God is not the absence of His light; it is the nearness of His body.

The nearness of His body is not a figure of speech; it is how shadows work, and Scripture builds a word on it.
The Hebrew for the __“image”__ of God in which man was made — _tselem_ (Genesis 1:26) — is built on _tsel_, the shade-word: an image is a shadow-figure, the outline a body casts.
With that in hand, return to the verse that opened this chapter:

[quote.scripture, Colossians 2:17]
____
Which are a *shadow of things to come*; but the body is of Christ.
____

The common teaching hears __“mere shadow”__ — and discards the sabbaths and feasts the verse is speaking of, as though Paul had called them worthless.
But a shadow is not detached from its body; it is _attached_ to it.
Where a shadow falls, a body stands, and a light shines behind it.

The law is __“a sym:sym-shadow[shadow] of *good things* to come”__ (Hebrews 10:1) — good things — and to keep the feast is to stand inside the outline of the Body that casts it, the way a man stands in the shadow of a great rock.
A shadow does not abolish its body, and a body does not abolish its shadow: they arrive together, and the shadow is precisely where the body is found.
Far from a warrant to discard, the shadow is the proof that the good things are real, near, and lit from behind by God.

The verse itself resists the discharge twice more.
Its command is __“let no man *judge you*”__ — protection for those keeping the holyday, the sym:sym-new-moon[new moon], and the sabbaths, not a sentence against them; the judges were the outsiders with their __“touch not; taste not”__ (Colossians 2:21), not the feasts.
And its tense is present while its object is future: the feasts __“*are*”__ — decades after the resurrection — __“a shadow of things *to come*”__: still casting, still pointing, the standing schedule of what remains.
A shadow ahead of a body means the body is still approaching; the appointed times are the outline of an arrival.

Ask whose arrival, for the verse answers in its last clause: __“the *body* is of Christ.”__
The shade is His Messiah.
Scripture had said so long before Colossae:

[quote.scripture, Lamentations 4:20]
____
The breath of our nostrils, the *anointed of the LORD*, was taken in their pits, of whom we said, *Under his shadow we shall live* among the heathen.
____

The Messiah's shadow is where His people live.
The bride sings the same: __“I sat down *under his shadow* with great delight, and his fruit was sweet to my taste”__ (Song of Solomon 2:3); and Isaiah's King is the shadow embodied — __“a *king* shall reign in sym:sym-righteousness[righteousness]… and *a man* shall be… as the *shadow of a great rock* in a weary land”__ (Isaiah 32:1-2), the great rock this chapter has been standing beside all along.
So the feasts are not a shadow *instead of* Christ; they are the shadow *of* Christ — cast by His body, falling where He stands — and the man who keeps them is standing in his Messiah's shade.

Now even the darkest use of the word gives up its comfort.
The __“shadow of death”__ — Hebrew _tsalmavet_, death’s shadow — is Death’s outline and boundary, not Death itself.

[quote.scripture, Psalm 23:4]
____
Yea, though I *walk through* the valley of the *shadow of death*, I will fear no evil: for *thou art with me*; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me.
____

Through — not into.
A sym:sym-valley[valley] is the low passage between sym:sym-mountain[mountains], and mountains are kingdoms: David crosses the border from Death’s kingdom of darkness toward the Shepherd’s kingdom of life (Colossians 1:13).
He does not belong to Death’s rule; the Shepherd guides him across its boundary.
God __“turneth the shadow of death into the morning”__ (Amos 5:8); He __“brought them out of sym:sym-darkness[darkness] and the shadow of death, and brake their bands in sunder”__ (Psalm 107:14); and on the people sitting __“in the region and shadow of death, sym:sym-light[light] is sprung up”__ (Isaiah 9:2; Matthew 4:16).
Wherever a shadow lies, a light is shining — the shadow of death itself testifies that the morning exists.
The rest of the word’s uses fall in line: our days pass __“as a shadow”__ (1 Chronicles 29:15; Psalm 144:4) because a shadow moves as the sym:sym-sun[sun] crosses — but with __“the Father of lights”__ there __“is no variableness, neither shadow of turning”__ (James 1:17): His shadow never moves off His people, because His light never moves.

Step back and take the lesson, because this chapter is a prime example of the whole method.
A word that nearly every reader carries as gloom is, by Scripture’s own usage, shelter: the Almighty’s wings, the kingdom’s tree, the overshadowing cloud, the law’s outline of good things to come, and even death reduced to a shadow with the morning behind it.
We recovered it the same way as always: gather every use, read the parallel columns, and treat the translators’ wobble — shadow here, __“defence”__ there — as a signpost to the Hebrew underneath.

It is good to be in the shadow.
The only question is whose.

sources.content:
---
title: "Mountain"
slug: mountain
order: 39
permalink: /books/meat-bibles-symbolic-language/mountain/
description: "Scripture defines the mountain as a kingdom — Revelation, Daniel, Isaiah, and Jeremiah agree — and that one key unlocks dozens of passages, from the burning mountain cast into the sea to the command to flee to the mountains."
og_title: "Mountain — MEAT The Bible's Symbolic Language"
epigraphs:
  - quote: "…the stone that smote the image became a great mountain, and filled the whole earth."
    ref: "Daniel 2:35"
---
The first case study is __“mountain,”__ which represents kingdoms or power structures.
The pyramid-like structure of a mountain mirrors the power structure of delegated authority and is an apt analogy — but subjective aptness is not a basis for defining a symbol.
Thankfully, in this case Scripture comes right out and defines it:

[quote.scripture, Revelation 17:9-10]
____
This calls for a mind with wisdom.
The seven heads are *seven mountains* on which the woman sits.
They are also *seven kings* (kingdoms).
____

Revelation tells us that mountains mean kingdoms, and by analogy hills are cities.
The question is whether Scripture consistently uses mountain with the same symbolic meaning, or whether this is a one-off.
Other times in Scripture we are given a vision and an interpretation, which establishes the definition by analogy:

[quote.scripture, Daniel 2:35 (NKJV)]
____
Then the iron, the clay, the bronze, the silver, and the gold were crushed together, and became like sym:sym-chaff[chaff] from the summer threshing floors; the sym:sym-wind[wind] carried them away so that no trace of them was found.
And the sym:sym-stone[stone] that struck the sym:sym-image[image] became a *great mountain* and *filled the whole earth*.
____

[quote.scripture, Daniel 2:44-45 (NKJV)]
____
And in the days of these kings the God of heaven will set up a *kingdom* which shall never be destroyed; and the kingdom shall not be left to other people; it shall break in pieces and *consume all these kingdoms*, and it shall stand forever.
Inasmuch as you saw that the sym:sym-stone[stone] was cut out of the *mountain* without hands, and that it broke in pieces the iron, the bronze, the clay, the silver, and the gold — the great God has made known to the king what will come to pass after this.
The dream is certain, and its interpretation is sure.
____

In this case Daniel explains a vision of a statue with layers of gold, silver, bronze, and feet of clay and iron, and explains that this statue represents successive kingdoms.
When God’s kingdom comes as a stone, it destroys the statue and consumes all the kingdoms the statue represents.
The stone then grows into a mountain that fills the entire earth, and God’s kingdom rules forever and ever.

[quote.scripture, Daniel 2:38-39 (NKJV)]
____
You are this head of gold.
After you shall arise another *kingdom* inferior to yours; then another, a third *kingdom* of bronze, which shall *rule over all the earth*.
____

Daniel's own explanation lets a ruler stand for the kingdom he heads: __“You are this head of gold,”__ followed immediately by __“another kingdom.”__
The sym:sym-stone[Stone] follows the same scale.
It enters the vision as one appointed Head and becomes the sym:sym-mountain[Mountain] as a people and kingdom gather under Him.

Rock and Stone are related, but they do not hold the same office.
The sym:sym-rock[Rock] is the bedrock beneath the house and kingdom — its sym:sym-covenant[covenant] Head, source, and foundation: __“that Rock was Christ”__ (1 Corinthians 10:4).
Isaiah gives the relationship at the human scale:

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 51:1-2]
____
Look unto the *rock whence ye are hewn*…
Look unto *Abraham your father*, and unto Sarah that bare you…
____

The rock is the father and source; the stones hewn from it are his people.
Peter carries the same order into the house of Christ: Jesus is the __“living sym:sym-stone[stone]”__ rejected by men, and those who come to Him __“also, as lively sym:sym-stone[stones], are built up a spiritual house”__ (1 Peter 2:4-5).
Jesus is the Rock beneath the house and the chief Stone within it; His people are the other living stones built under His authority.

The chief corner stone is the *Head* in authority while remaining at the foundation in position.
Isaiah lays the tried corner stone __“for a foundation”__ (Isaiah 28:16), and Paul says the house is __“built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone”__ (Ephesians 2:20).
Placed at the foundation corner, the Head Stone establishes the line to which every other stone must be fitted.
Zechariah's physically upper stone uses a different expression: Psalm 118:22 calls Christ _rosh pinnah_, __“the head of the corner,”__ while Zechariah 4:7 calls the completing top stone _ha-even ha-roshah_, __“the headstone.”__
The cornerstone governs the building from beneath; the capstone crowns it from above.

Daniel's sym:sym-stone[Stone] cut without hands is therefore Christ as the Head appointed by God, not a kingdom assembled by men.
As the living stones are built under Him, the single Stone becomes the great Mountain — the kingdom that fills the earth.

The fact that the mountain is described as growing and covering the entire earth is another clue that this isn’t a physical mountain.
The analogy from Daniel is carried on in Isaiah.

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 2:2-3]
____
It shall come to pass in the latter days that the *mountain* of the house of the Lord shall be established as the highest of the *mountains*, and shall be lifted up above the *hills*; and all the *nations* shall flow to it, and many peoples shall come.
____

See the same symbolic meaning applied in Jeremiah, describing Babylon the Great, which rules over the whole earth and destroys nation after nation.
Here Jeremiah tells us this destroying mountain will become a burnt mountain.

[quote.scripture, Jeremiah 51:25]
____
Behold, I am against you, O *destroying mountain*, Who destroys all the earth,” says the Lord.
“And I will stretch out My hand against you, Roll you down from the rocks, And make you a *burnt mountain*.
____

Now we have Daniel, Revelation, Isaiah, and Jeremiah all agreeing on the meaning of this symbol of a Mountain as a Kingdom.
With this knowledge we can now gain greater insight into many other Scriptures.
Consider the account in Revelation of a flaming mountain thrown into the sea:

[quote.scripture, Revelation 8:8-9]
____
Then the second angel sounded his trumpet, and something like a *huge mountain*, all ablaze, was *thrown into the* sym:sym-sea[sea].
A third of the *sea* turned into blood, a third of the *living creatures* in the sea died….
____

The common readings rank this way:

.How the “mountain” is usually read (Revelation 8:8)
[.prevalence-table%unbreakable, frame=topbot, grid=none, cols="^2,8", options="header"]
|===
| Rank | Common interpretation

| 1 | Literal asteroid or meteor impact
| 2 | Literal volcano hurled into the sea
| 3 | Nuclear blast or modern warfare
| 4 | A nation or world empire
|===

How do we know that this isn’t a literal mountain in this context?
The answer is in the phrase __“thrown into the sea,”__ the __“sea turning into blood,”__ and the __“creatures in the sea,”__ all in the same sentence.
In a later chapter I will show the evidence that sym:sym-sea[sea] is a symbol that means the masses of people, the population of the earth, and that sym:sym-living[living creatures], sym:sym-beast[beast], and sym:sym-beast[animals] represent gentile nations.

Symbolically, Revelation 8:8-9 is saying that when a __“huge mountain”__ — a world empire — is thrown down, a third of the people will die and a third of the nations will be destroyed.

One final supporting piece of evidence is that a __“stone, rock, mountain, etc.”__ being __“thrown into the sea”__ to __“never rise again”__ is the prophetic symbol tied to the fall of Babylon the Great.
And thus symbols can be composed of both words and catchphrases.

[quote.scripture, Matthew 17:20]
____
So Jesus said to them, “Because of your unbelief; for assuredly, I say to you, if you have sym:sym-faith[faith] *as a mustard* sym:sym-seed[seed], you will say to this *mountain*, ‘Move from here to there,’ and it will move; and nothing will be impossible for you.”
____

[quote.scripture, Matthew 21:21]
____
So Jesus answered and said to them, “Assuredly, I say to you, if you have sym:sym-faith[faith] and do not doubt, you will not only do what was done to the sym:sym-fig[*fig tree*], but also if you say to this *mountain*, ‘Be removed and be *cast into the* sym:sym-sea[sea],’ it will be done.”
____

[quote.scripture, Mark 11:23]
____
For assuredly, I say to you, whoever says to this *mountain*, ‘Be removed and be *cast into the sea*,’ and does not doubt in his heart, but believes that those things he says will be done, he will have whatever he says.
____

The common readings rank this way:

.How the “mountain” Jesus moves is usually read
[.prevalence-table%unbreakable, frame=topbot, grid=none, cols="^2,8", options="header"]
|===
| Rank | Common interpretation

| 1 | A personal obstacle or problem
| 2 | A literal mountain, used as hyperbole
| 3 | The Mount of Olives or Temple Mount
| 4 | A spiritual stronghold or doubt
| 5 | The corrupt temple or religious system
| 6 | A national power or kingdom
|===

How do we know that this mountain is not a literal mountain, or merely an impossible obstacle, in this context?
Because the context is a fig tree and a mustard tree — and sym:sym-tree[trees] are rooted covenant lives that can stand for peoples or nations — and of course __“thrown into the sea”__ is a symbol clearly referring to Babylon the Great, as the link:/books/symbolic-language/the-fall-of-babylon/[Fall of Babylon] chapter demonstrated — and as the next chapter will trace from the Song of the Sea onward.

What we learn from this is that the symbolic language of the Bible is interconnected: symbols are defined in terms of symbols and phrases, as well as the verbs, adjectives, and other personifications used with the symbol.
For this reason, we often see the same set of symbols connected over and over.

[quote.scripture, Psalm 46:2-3]
____
Though the *mountains* be carried into the midst of the sym:sym-sea[sea]; though the waters thereof roar and be troubled, though the *mountains* shake with the swelling thereof.
____

The common readings rank this way:

.How the “mountains” are usually read (Psalm 46)
[.prevalence-table%unbreakable, frame=topbot, grid=none, cols="^2,8", options="header"]
|===
| Rank | Common interpretation

| 1 | Literal earthquakes or natural disaster
| 2 | Life’s troubles and instability
| 3 | Cosmic or end-times upheaval
| 4 | Nations or kingdoms shaken
|===

Now consider this poetic picture from Joel:

[quote.scripture, Joel 2:2]
____
A day of darkness and gloom, A day of clouds and of thick [dark] mist, Like the *dawn* spread over the *mountains*;
____

The picture is of __“dawn,”__ __“mist,”__ or __“fog”__ spread over the __“mountains,”__ which is quite common in early morning and aligns with the visual of a __“day of clouds and thick dark mist.”__
The Hebrew word for __“dawn,”__ _shachar_, link:/books/symbolic-language/lucifers-declared-plan/[names the dark before sunrise].footnote:fn33shachar[Derived — _shachar_ written on the letters of blackness — in the link:/books/symbolic-language/lucifers-declared-plan/[Lucifer's Declared Plan] chapter.] It names the first light while the sky is still quite dark, before the sun burns away the fog.
Now, with the greater context, we have dark clouds of smoke spread over the nations.
This is just one of dozens of verses that gain new meaning when you apply the symbolic meaning of mountain.

[quote.scripture, Matthew 24:15-16]
____
So when you see the abomination of desolation spoken of by the prophet Daniel, standing in the holy place (let the reader understand), then let those who are in Judea *flee to the mountains*.
____

Here is a verse that contains instructions for the future, and to understand the instructions it is helpful to know that __“mountains”__ means nations.
In other words: get out of Judea.
In AD 70, those who survived the fall of Jerusalem were scattered to the nations, so this prophecy has been fulfilled in this sense already.

[quote.scripture, Luke 21:20-21]
____
When you see Jerusalem being surrounded by armies, you will know that its desolation is near.
Then let those who are in Judea *flee to the mountains*, let those in the *city* get out, and let those in the country not enter the city.
____

Another verse sounds poetic on the surface, but carries a far more practical message when read by Scripture’s own symbols:

[quote.scripture, Jeremiah 50:6]
____
My people have been sym:sym-lost[lost sheep]; their *shepherds* have led them astray, in the *mountains* they have turned them away. *From mountain to hill* they have gone; they have forgotten their resting place.
____

Here His people are the sheep; the shepherds are the pastors and teachers who led people astray among the nations they were scattered to.
His people have gone from nation to city and have forgotten their home.

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 40:4]
____
Every sym:sym-valley[valley] shall be exalted, and every *mountain and hill* shall be made low.
____

This verse from Isaiah now has far deeper meaning: the nations and cities will be humbled (brought low).
And those who are humble, obedient even to death, will be exalted and lifted up.
The mountains are high places, proud places, and they contrast with their opposite, the valleys — those enslaved by the mountains.

[quote.scripture, Jeremiah 16:16]
____
Behold, I will send for many *fishers*, said the LORD, and they shall fish them; and after will I send for many *hunters*, and they shall hunt them from *every mountain*, and from *every hill*, and out of the *holes of the rocks*.
____

Here is another case where mountains (nations) are used with other symbols: fishermen and hunters.
Here Jeremiah is prophesying about Jesus calling people to be fishers of men.
Then, those who are not caught as fish will be hunted down from among the nations, in every city, and out of every bunker.
The holes of the rocks are then referenced in Revelation:

[quote.scripture, Revelation 6:14-16]
____
And the heaven departed as a scroll when it is rolled together; and *every mountain and* sym:sym-island[island] were moved out of their places.
And the kings of the earth, and the great men, and the rich men, and the chief captains, and the mighty men, and every slave, and every free man, hid themselves in the dens and in the *rocks of the mountains*; and said to the *mountains and rocks*, Fall on us, and hide us.
____

Now that you know that mountain means a kingdom, we should ask ourselves: what does an sym:sym-island[island] represent?

[quote.scripture, Revelation 16:19-20]
____
And great *Babylon* came in remembrance before God, to give to her the cup of the wine of the fierceness of his wrath.
And *every* sym:sym-island[island] *fled away*, and the *mountains were not found*.
____

Are literal mountains going to disappear, or is this clearly talking about the third of the nations thrown into the sea, never to rise again?
When I read this, it struck me as odd that an island could flee, or escape.
It is the personification of the island that led me to research the sym:sym-island[island] symbol, which we will cover in a future chapter.

I will close this chapter on mountains with one final notable use, when Jesus was tested in the desert:

[quote.scripture, Matthew 4:8]
____
Again, the devil takes him up into an *exceeding high mountain*, and shows him *all the kingdoms of the world*, and the glory of them;
____

Here we see an exceedingly high mountain from which all the other kingdoms of the earth can be seen.
In other words, he is taken to a kingdom ruling over all the other kings of the earth — likely Babylon the Great.

By now you should see the pattern: Scripture reliably and consistently uses the word mountain as a way to say __“nation”__ or __“kingdom”__ in many different contexts across the whole of Scripture.
I have only addressed a few of the notable uses, but once you internalize this symbol you will find it used in countless other places in profound ways.

In the process of exploring the mountain symbol, we came across many other symbols: the sym:sym-sea[sea] (the masses of mankind), the hills (cities), the sym:sym-tree[tree] and the fig tree (kingdoms and Israel), the sym:sym-stone[stones] (people built into a house), the sym:sym-rock[Rock] (Christ, the foundation beneath it), the sym:sym-beast[beasts] and living creatures (the gentile nations), the sym:sym-island[island], the fishers and the hunters, the valley, and Babylon the Great.
The sea, the trees and their beasts, and the island are taken up in the chapters just ahead, each defined the same way we defined the mountain — by letting Scripture interpret Scripture.
Babylon the Great we have already traced through Part Five, and the glossary carries the rest.

The meaning is already there, recoverable by following the repeated relationships rather than leaning on inherited opinion.
What forces the answer is not the cleverness of the reader but the discipline of the process.
